Content:
Suppose that we have [MATH: 10] stamps worth [MATH: \color{blue}3] cents each and [MATH: 4] stamps worth [MATH: \color{blue}5] cents each.
We can compute the total value of our stamps by multiplying the value of each stamp by its quantity and then adding the totals.
[MATH: \underbrace{ \hspace{.25cm} \color{blue}3 \text{ cents} \hspace{.25cm} }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{10}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} + \underbrace{\hspace{.25cm} \color{blue}5 \text{ cents} \hspace{.25cm} }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{4}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} = 50 \text{ cents}]

Content:
We can use this principle to set up equations for problems involving items with monetary values.

Content:
For example, if we have [MATH: a] stamps worth [MATH: 3] cents each and [MATH: b] stamps worth [MATH: 5] cents each, and the total cost of all the stamps is [MATH: 80] cents, then
[MATH: \underbrace{\color{blue}3}_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{a}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} + \underbrace{\color{blue}5}_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{b}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} = 80]
Also, if we know that there are [MATH: 16] stamps in total, then we have
[MATH: a+b=16.]
Therefore, we can represent this problem as the following system of equations in the unknowns [MATH: a] and [MATH: b\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {3a + 5b = 80; a + b = 16]

Content:
This system can be solved using substitution or elimination.

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: p] be the number of pennies and [MATH: n] the number of nickels in the wallet.

  • There are [MATH: 16] coins in total, so [MATH: p+n=16.]

  • Each penny is worth [MATH: 1] cent, each nickel is worth [MATH: 5] cents, and the total value of all the coins is [MATH: 56] cents, so [MATH: p+5n=56.]

Putting these equations together, we have the following system of equations:

[MATH: {p + n = 16; p + 5n = 56]

We will solve the system using elimination. Multiplying the first equation by [MATH: -1] and adding the result to the second equation, we solve for [MATH: n\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: − p − n|= − 16; p + 5n|= 56; 4n|= 40; n|= 10]

To find [MATH: p,] we substitute [MATH: n=10] into the first equation:

[MATH: p + n|= 16; p + (10)|= 16; p|= 6]

The solution to the system is [MATH: p=6] and [MATH: n=10.] Therefore, there are [MATH: 6] pennies and [MATH: 10] nickels in the wallet.

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: x] be the number of cereal boxes, and [MATH: y] be the number of pasta boxes.

  • Each box of cereal costs [MATH: \[math]3,] each box of pasta costs [MATH: \[/math]5,] and Ross spent [MATH: \[math]27,] so [MATH: 3x+5y=27.]

  • Ross bought a total of [MATH: 7] items, so [MATH: x+y=7.]

Putting these equations together, we have the following system of equations:

[MATH: 3x + 5y = 27; x + y = 7]

We will solve the system using elimination. Multiplying the second equation by [MATH: -3] and adding the result to the first equation, we solve for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 3x + 5y|= 27; − 3x − 3y|= − 21; 2y|= 6; y|= 3]

Therefore, Ross bought [MATH: 3] boxes of pasta.

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: x] be the price of a kilogram of apples and [MATH: y] the price of a kilogram of plums.

  • The combined price of [MATH: 3\,\mathrm{kg}] of apples and [MATH: 2\,\mathrm{kg}] of plums is [MATH: \[math]12,] so [MATH: 3x + 2y = 12.]

  • The combined price of [MATH: 2\,\mathrm{kg}] of plums and [MATH: 1\,\mathrm{kg}] of apples is [MATH: \[/math]8], so [MATH: x+2y = 8.]

Putting these equations together, we have the following system of equations:

[MATH: {3x + 2y = 12; x + 2y = 8]

We will solve the system using substitution. We solve for [MATH: x] in the second equation:

[MATH: 2y + x|= 8; x|= 8 − 2y]

Then, we can substitute [MATH: x=8-2y] into the first equation and solve for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 3x + 2y|= 12; 3(8 − 2y) + 2y|= 12; 24 − 6y + 2y|= 12; 24 − 4y|= 12; − 4y|= − 12; y|= 3]

Therefore, a kilogram of plums costs [MATH: \[math]3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we have [MATH: 10] stamps worth [MATH: \color{blue}3] cents each and [MATH: 4] stamps worth [MATH: \color{blue}5] cents each.
We can compute the total value of our stamps by multiplying the value of each stamp by its quantity and then adding the totals.
[MATH: \underbrace{ \hspace{.25cm} \color{blue}3 \text{ cents} \hspace{.25cm} }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{10}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} + \underbrace{\hspace{.25cm} \color{blue}5 \text{ cents} \hspace{.25cm} }_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{4}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} = 50 \text{ cents}]

Content:
We can use this principle to set up equations for problems involving items with monetary values.

Content:
For example, if we have [MATH: a] stamps worth [MATH: 3] cents each and [MATH: b] stamps worth [MATH: 5] cents each, and the total cost of all the stamps is [MATH: 80] cents, then
[MATH: \underbrace{\color{blue}3}_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{a}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} + \underbrace{\color{blue}5}_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{value}} \times \overbrace{b}^{\large\textrm{quantity}} = 80]
Also, if we know that there are [MATH: 16] stamps in total, then we have
[MATH: a+b=16.]
Therefore, we can represent this problem as the following system of equations in the unknowns [MATH: a] and [MATH: b\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: {3a + 5b = 80; a + b = 16]

This system can be solved using substitution or elimination.

Item 2 — Tutorial: United States Currency

- Coins come in the following denominations:

[MATH: \quad] [MATH: 1]-cent - called a penny

Item 3 — Example: Solving for a Quantity of Coins

Example Prompt:
A wallet contains pennies ([MATH: 1]-cent coins) and nickels ([MATH: 5]-cent coins). There are [MATH: 16] coins in total. If the total amount of money in the wallet is [MATH: \[math]0.56], how many of each coin are there?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: p] be the number of pennies and [MATH: n] the number of nickels in the wallet.

- There are [MATH: 16] coins in total, so [MATH: p+n=16.]
- Each penny is worth [MATH: 1] cent, each nickel is worth [MATH: 5] cents, and the total value of all the coins is [MATH: 56] cents, so [MATH: p+5n=56.]

Putting these equations together, we have the following system of equations:

[MATH: {p + n = 16; p + 5n = 56]

We will solve the system using elimination. Multiplying the first equation by [MATH: -1] and adding the result to the second equation, we solve for [MATH: n\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: − p − n|= − 16; p + 5n|= 56; 4n|= 40; n|= 10]

To find [MATH: p,] we substitute [MATH: n=10] into the first equation:

[MATH: p + n|= 16; p + (10)|= 16; p|= 6]

The solution to the system is [MATH: p=6] and [MATH: n=10.] Therefore, there are [MATH: 6] pennies and [MATH: 10] nickels in the wallet.

Item 6 — Example: Solving for a Quantity of Items

Example Prompt:
In a store, a box of cereal is [MATH: \[math]3], while a box of pasta is [MATH: \[/math]5.] Ross spends [MATH: \[math]27] on boxes of cereal and pasta. If Ross buys a total of [MATH: 7] items, how many boxes of pasta does he buy?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: x] be the number of cereal boxes, and [MATH: y] be the number of pasta boxes.

- Each box of cereal costs [MATH: \[math]3,] each box of pasta costs [MATH: \[/math]5,] and Ross spent [MATH: \[math]27,] so [MATH: 3x+5y=27.]
- Ross bought a total of [MATH: 7] items, so [MATH: x+y=7.]

Putting these equations together, we have the following system of equations:

[MATH: 3x + 5y = 27; x + y = 7]

We will solve the system using elimination. Multiplying the second equation by [MATH: -3] and adding the result to the first equation, we solve for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 3x + 5y|= 27; − 3x − 3y|= − 21; 2y|= 6; y|= 3]

Therefore, Ross bought [MATH: 3] boxes of pasta.

Item 9 — Example: Solving for a Value

Example Prompt:
A store sells a bag containing [MATH: 3\,\mathrm{kg}] of apples and [MATH: 2\,\mathrm{kg}] of plums for [MATH: \[math]12.] If the combined price of [MATH: 2\,\mathrm{kg}] of plums and [MATH: 1\,\mathrm{kg}] of apples is [MATH: \[/math]8], how much does a kilogram of plums cost?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: x] be the price of a kilogram of apples and [MATH: y] the price of a kilogram of plums.

- The combined price of [MATH: 3\,\mathrm{kg}] of apples and [MATH: 2\,\mathrm{kg}] of plums is [MATH: \[math]12,] so [MATH: 3x + 2y = 12.]
- The combined price of [MATH: 2\,\mathrm{kg}] of plums and [MATH: 1\,\mathrm{kg}] of apples is [MATH: \[/math]8], so [MATH: x+2y = 8.]

Putting these equations together, we have the following system of equations:

[MATH: {3x + 2y = 12; x + 2y = 8]

We will solve the system using substitution. We solve for [MATH: x] in the second equation:

[MATH: 2y + x|= 8; x|= 8 − 2y]

Then, we can substitute [MATH: x=8-2y] into the first equation and solve for [MATH: y\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: 3x + 2y|= 12; 3(8 − 2y) + 2y|= 12; 24 − 6y + 2y|= 12; 24 − 4y|= 12; − 4y|= − 12; y|= 3]

Therefore, a kilogram of plums costs [MATH: \[math]3.]
